items.body: John Coltrane – The John Coltrane Quartet Plays (Impulse, 1965) By Dan Sorrells Most of my listening hours are spent on freely improvised music. But when it comes to Coltrane, I love the classic quartet, 1965, right before things broke open (and the group, apart). The John Coltrane Quartet Plays is what I reach for most often. “Chim Chim Cheree” starts like another “My Favorite Things,” but less than a minute in, Coltrane’s already chafing against the melody, and after two he and Jones are fairly bursting out of Tyner’s measured vamp. “Brazilia” and “Nature Boy” enticingly point toward the searching explorations to come, where ideas were turned inside-out in dizzying, kaleidoscopic epics (something further evidenced by various surfaced recordings from the Half Note during the same period, where “Chim” and “Song of Praise” stretch to twice the length). The sense that traditional song forms must still be made to contain Trane’s increasingly frenetic probing lends indelible tension to the music; these songs are like swelling water ballons, but they’re filled with boiling water. For those of us in the future, it’s all the more heightened when you know just how far things will get pushed, even before the close of the year. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop spaces, but the moods blossom into an entirely new ecosystem. The inclusion of Eric Dolphy was one of Trane’s most brilliant moves. On Naima, Spiritual, India , his low horns (also sax and bass clarinet) perfectly match Trane’s tenor and soprano sax. Trane’s interest in alternative spiritual and musical traditions is obvious enough. His famous “sheets of sound” slide in and out of every line. I find the articulation of Coltrane’s own personality to be as vivid here as on any of his recordings. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Music has been a lifelong companion for Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong, beginning with a birthday present from his late father when he was young.

Speaking at the JASS Benefit Gala 2026 on 26 September, Wong reflected on his early experiences with music, his fascination with jazz, and how playing music has helped him connect with people from different backgrounds.

“Music has always been a big part of my life,” Wong said, sharing that he did not grow up with formal music training.

Instead, his introduction to playing came after his late father gave him a guitar as a birthday present. A friend of his father, whom Wong described as a skilled player, subsequently taught him informally.

The guitar would later follow Wong halfway around the world when he left Singapore to attend university in the United States in the early ‘90s.

There, he met his American roommate, who grew up on a farm in rural Wisconsin. Wong recalled wondering how they would get along given their vastly different backgrounds — until he discovered they had something important in common.

His roommate had brought a guitar with him, and Wong had brought his own from Singapore.

“We clicked immediately,” Wong recalled. The pair began jamming together on their first night and were busking together just days later.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

For Wong, the encounter demonstrated music’s ability to bridge differences.

“You don't need to come from the same place or have very much in common,” he said. “Once you start playing together, you find a common language.”

On jazz and listening to one another

Wong also spoke about his interest in jazz, sharing that he enjoys classic standards and has tried playing the genre himself.

He admitted that jazz can sometimes feel intimidating without formal training because of its technical demands. But beyond its complexity, Wong said what appealed to him was the way musicians listened and responded to one another.

He described jazz as giving musicians the freedom to improvise within a structure — picking up on each other’s ideas and collectively taking the music somewhere new.

To Wong, that spirit extends beyond jazz.

He drew parallels with Singapore’s Chinese, Malay, and Indian musical traditions, describing the country as a natural meeting point for different cultures and influences.

“Our multiculturalism is not about making everything the same,” Wong said, pointing instead to how different strands can be mixed and adapted to create something distinctive.

He highlighted the work of Jazz Association (Singapore) (JASS) in bringing jazz together with Asian musical traditions and instruments, as the organisation celebrated its 10th anniversary at the gala.

Looking to the future, Wong encouraged JASS to keep jazz accessible, continue experimenting with different cultural influences, and bring musicians from different backgrounds together.

He also called for more opportunities for young musicians in Singapore to “create, explore and innovate”.

“Importantly, let's continue to bring people together through music,” he said.

Jazz Association (Singapore) (JASS) raised S$1,436,096 at its Benefit Gala 2026, When You Wish Upon A Star – A Decade of Dreams, on 26 September, with donations going towards music education, community outreach, youth development, and support for musicians.

Held at Shangri-La Singapore, the gala marked JASS’ 10th anniversary and brought together the organisation’s musicians, supporters, and young talents for an evening celebrating a decade of Singapore jazz.

Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong joined the celebration as Guest of Honour and delivered a heartfelt speech during the evening.

Music took centre stage with performances spanning generations of Singapore’s jazz community. Maya Raisha, a recipient of the JASS Music Scholarship 2025, opened the night, while renowned vocalist Teresa Carpio took to the stage later in the evening.

The celebration culminated in a finale featuring Carpio alongside a combined Jazz Association Singapore Orchestra (JASSO) and Jazz Association Singapore Youth Orchestra (JASSYO!) ensemble, led by JASS Executive Director and Music Director Professor Jeremy Monteiro.

The evening also featured the presentation of the JASS Appreciation Awards, JASS Ambassador Awards, and JASS Philanthropy Awards, as well as the “Power of Love” pledge ahead of the announcement of the night’s fundraising total.

A decade of growing Singapore jazz

Founded in 2016 by Monteiro, Albert Chiu, Dr Edmund Lam, and Susan Peh, JASS was established to expand Singapore’s jazz community, advance music education through scholarships, and bring jazz to wider audiences in Singapore and abroad.

Over its first decade, the organisation has raised more than S$6.3 million to support its programmes and activities. More than 220 musicians have performed across JASS concerts, festivals, and community programmes, while over 110 young musicians have gained stage experience and mentorship through JASSYO!.

Its work in music education has also grown significantly. Since the JASS Music Scholarship was established in 2018, more than S$500,000 has been invested in the programme, with 15 scholarships awarded as of 31 March.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Jazz Association (Singapore) (@jazzassociation_sg)

This year, JASS expanded its youth development efforts with JASS Junior, an initiative for musicians aged 18 and below that offers private coaching, mentored ensemble rehearsals, and performance-based learning opportunities.

The association also established the JASS Catalyst Fund in April to support Singapore’s jazz community across professional development, recording projects, and overseas performances.

Taking Singapore jazz beyond home shores

JASS’ work over the past decade has extended beyond Singapore. Since JASSO made its international debut at the JZ Shanghai Jazz Festival in 2017, the association has staged 13 international performances across seven countries and eight cities.

Its musicians have taken Singapore jazz to stages in Australia, South Korea, China, Thailand, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Closer to home, JASS has presented 114 signature productions and 50 community events while creating 39 original compositions and 151 new arrangements. Its international collaborations have included jazz artists Randy Brecker, Benny Golson, Carmen Bradford, Laura Fygi, and Roberta Gambarini.

The S$1,436,096 raised at the anniversary gala will now go towards continuing the programmes that have shaped JASS’ first decade — from developing young talent and creating educational opportunities to supporting professional musicians and bringing jazz to communities across Singapore.

The gala concluded with a 10th-anniversary cake-cutting, followed by a dance set led by JASS Deputy Music Director Chok Kerong, featuring Maya Raisha and the combined orchestra.

items.body:
Fresh off a high-octane set at MARQUEE Singapore, Sub Zero Project are showing no signs of slowing down. More than a decade into their journey, the Dutch duo of Nigel Coppen and Thomas Velderman continue to push hardstyle in new directions, pairing their unmistakable sound with increasingly ambitious live concepts and collaborations.

That momentum has carried through Our World, their latest audiovisual live concept, as well as 4444 OF A KIND, their four-man project with D-Block & S-te-Fan. Their growing presence across Tomorrowland and recent collaboration with Steve Aoki on 'Promises' have also placed them firmly within a wider electronic music conversation at a time when, as the duo put it, genre boundaries are beginning to fade.

Following their explosive performance at the Marina Bay Sands megaclub, Bandwagon caught up with Sub Zero Project to talk about 4444 OF A KIND, their approach to hardstyle, the creative freedom behind their live concepts, working with Steve Aoki, and more.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

You’ve spent more than a decade making music together. When you listen back to your earliest productions, what do you hear that is still unmistakably Sub Zero Project today?

We hear the same drive to experiment and push the boundaries of hard dance that we still have today. Of course, our sound has changed a lot over the years, but we always want to come up with something fresh. We believe that this is what has made our sound recognisable over the years.

You’ve worked together for so long that fans often experience Sub Zero Project as one creative unit. What are Nigel and Thomas individually bringing to the studio that the other person probably couldn’t replicate?

Even though we always work together on music, we definitely have different strengths in the studio. Thomas is more focused on melodies and the musical side of a track, while Nigel has a strong focus on the technical side, like kicks and other small details such as sound design and creative ideas. Those different strengths complement each other really well and are a big part of how we work together.

You’ve built Our World around four distinct visual worlds alongside new music created for this chapter of Sub Zero Project. How did you come up with the concept, and how does building a narrative-driven live show affect the way you create music in the studio?

With Our World, we wanted to show people what “Our World” actually stands for, which could be anything, just like our music. Instead of coming up with one specific theme for our show, we wanted to combine very different themes and styles into one show. The same goes for our music.

It was a really fun creative process setting up this show and creating all the music that came with it. We brought the show to so many incredible places like Antwerp, Gothenburg, Mexico City, Paris, and many more.

You’ve created several distinct live concepts over the years instead of simply touring the same DJ show. What have these concepts allowed you to express that a normal Sub Zero Project festival set cannot?

The biggest difference is that our live concepts allow us to bring our full vision to life. It’s not just about the music anymore — it’s the visuals, production, and show coming together as one experience.

It also gives us a different way to work on music. We’ve always been at our best if we have a certain direction or theme that we can dive into.

4444 OF A KIND brings you together with D-Block & S-te-Fan as a dedicated four-person team rather than simply another collaboration. Its debut single, 'Waiting 4', arrived in June, following years of history between both duos. At what point did you realise there was enough chemistry between the four of you to build an entirely new identity around it?

We actually already knew this back when we made our first collaboration, 'Darkest Hour', in 2018. The chemistry was instantly there.

Fast-forward to the end of 2025, when our management came up with the idea to build a new identity between Sub Zero Project and D-Block & S-te-Fan called 4444 OF A KIND. We already knew it was going to be a smooth and fun ride working on new music.

We spent three days at a writing camp together and made more than 10 songs, which was an amazing experience.

'Darkest Hour (The Clock)' already showed how naturally your two sounds could meet. With 4444 OF A KIND, however, you’re creating music specifically as one project. What happens differently in the studio when four producers with very established identities have to decide what a new artist should sound like?

Complete creative freedom happens. With 4444 OF A KIND, we don’t go into the studio thinking, “We have to make a new Sub Zero Project or D-Block & S-te-Fan song.”

Instead, we just have fun, come up with cool stuff, and see where the process takes us. This new project is about pushing the boundaries of hard dance and playing with different genres, without limiting ourselves to one specific sound.

This year, you had a huge presence at Tomorrowland — playing the Mainstage, hosting Sub Zero Project & Friends, performing as 4444 OF A KIND, and going back-to-back with Hardwell. From your perspective, is hardstyle having a broader global moment right now, or are the boundaries between hardstyle and mainstream electronic music simply disappearing?

We definitely feel that boundaries are fading more and more. People don’t really think in genres as much as they did back in the day, which is a good thing in our opinion, and it makes it easier for certain EDM artists to play harder songs.

For us, this is an incredibly exciting time to be a music producer.

Finally, collaboration with Steve Aoki, 'Promises', reimagines NERO’s 2011 track. What made you want to revisit that particular record, and why was Steve Aoki the right producer for you to team up with?

We absolutely love the original, so once we started chatting with him, we both agreed we could do something epic with this song. We have a good connection with Steve, and this collaboration was long overdue. We’re very happy we could finally make it happen.

items.body:
At 12, Anastasha Suchin is already learning how many stories a violin can tell. She started playing at three and a half, and has since taken the instrument from concert stages to Singapore’s National Day celebrations, where she performed her own arrangement bringing together Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil songs. She has also stepped into composition with Rosie, a miniature horror tale written for toy piano and performed by Margaret Leng Tan.

Her latest chapter brought her to the big screen. In Singapore-led animated feature The Violinist, Anastasha performs as young Fei, recording pieces by Paganini and Mendelssohn alongside original music for the film. The experience saw her approach the violin not simply as a performer, but as the musical voice of a character whose story unfolds against the Japanese Occupation.

Music has taken on an even more personal role away from the stage. With her father currently in hospital, Anastasha sometimes plays for him at his bedside — continuing a relationship with music that began when he used to ferry her to violin lessons as a child. Speaking to Bandwagon, she reflects on composing Rosie, hearing herself in The Violinist for the first time, balancing school with music, and why making someone smile remains the reason she plays.

You started learning the violin when you were very young. What do you remember about first picking it up, and what made you want to keep playing?

When I was three and a half, Mum decided to let me start on the violin, as she plays the piano and envisioned us playing many duets in the future. So it was chosen for me, but I took to it very naturally and was glad to have had a nurturing and friendly first teacher, so that made me look forward to going for classes each week.

It probably did sound like “sawing wood” at first, but I’ve improved since then.

You’re balancing school, violin practice, performances, and your other interests at just 12 years old. What does a typical week look like for you, and how do you make time for everything?

I am tuition-free, and that gives me space to relax when I get home. Co-Curricular Activity days are long ones — I am in the String Ensemble at Tanjong Katong Girls’ School — and I get home at 7 PM several days a week.

I love playing with my 16-year-old black cat and am right now in the phase of experimenting with bakes and concocting fancy drinks. Practising has never been a strong point of mine. I should be able to say that I work on my instrument for several hours a day, but in truth, I actually don’t.

Instead, I tinker on the piano and guitar and also love to sing. Oops, I hope my violin teacher (Ye Lin) isn’t reading this! Sometimes I go thrift shopping on the weekends after visiting my father in hospital.

However, when I know there is an upcoming performance, I will definitely put in the time needed to do a good job on the day. Just like studying for an exam, I guess, but much more fun.

Last year, you performed a special National Day arrangement that brought together Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil songs. How did you choose those songs, and what did you want people to feel when they heard them together?

Not only am I biracial, I also have a lot of Indian friends. Our family’s favourite food is chicken biryani! I wanted each race to be represented in my little medley.

It was an easy choice — I simply selected my three favourite songs, one in each language, to make into one. My hope was to make everyone feel included and put a big smile in their hearts.

You also composed Rosie, which has since been performed internationally. Where did the idea for the piece come from, and what did creating your own musical story teach you that performing someone else’s music could not?

Rosie was composed in 2024, when I was 10.

I’ve always been fascinated by the beaked masks the Plague Doctors wore. When the request came in for an original composition to be performed by the legendary artist Margaret Leng Tan on toy piano at the Green-Wood Catacombs — on Halloween! — it seemed like the perfect opportunity to write music based on the imagery which the mask evoked.

The more I worked on it, the more it evolved, eventually becoming a miniature horror tale in four parts, including the actual use of the mask, among other accessories!

I felt free to create the story which I wanted, with full creative licence and no performance time limits. When performing someone else’s work, every dot and dash has to be observed to give respect to the composer’s intentions. So that would be the main difference between being a composer and a performer.

How did you first become involved with The Violinist, and what did you know about young Fei when you came on board?

My manager read the press release about the upcoming movie The Violinist earlier in 2025 and, by chance, the accompanying illustration of Fei resembled me! She reached out to the director, Mr Ervin, and composer, Mr Ricky, and things fell into place from there on!

We were told that Fei was a young Peranakan girl who was prodigious on the violin, and that this story was set during the Japanese Occupation.

My grandma was actually born in the forest while great-grandma ran away from troops in 1941. My grandpa’s father disappeared during the war, and it was tough days for grandpa growing up then too. These stories resonated with me.

It is very exciting to have been blessed with the part of young Fei and have a small role in this Singapore story. I still haven’t gotten over it yet!

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by 🎻 Anastasha Suchin (@anastasha.suchin.violin)

What was your role in bringing young Fei to life musically, and what was the recording process like?

Mr Ricky Ho gave me a list of pieces I had to prepare for the recording. It included the super well-known Paganini Caprice No. 24 and the opening of the Mendelssohn Violin Concerto. These are works which I grew up hearing great artists play so flawlessly. Pressure was high, but I knew I would give it my best!

There was also a lovely original duet to be performed by Fei and Kai, and that was really fun for us to do as a first-time collaboration with Mark Chia. We got along really well and also had the chance to meet up again later in Vienna, where we visited Haus der Musik together!

When you were playing as Fei, did you have to imagine how this particular character would sound on the violin, rather than simply playing as yourself?

I recorded Fei’s parts over two sessions — once with Mark at YST Recording Studio in August 2025 and later on, solo at HORUS Studios, where I did the Paganini and the Mendelssohn.

Mr Ricky told me to play as myself, since I was meant to sound like Fei practising and not a seasoned adult professional violinist performing. That was very helpful in making me play more naturally.

An interesting story is that I had literally just transitioned to a full-size violin the day before recording the duet. A benefactor who wishes to remain anonymous had generously sponsored my beautiful new instrument as I was outgrowing my current one.

An Italian luthier had made one for me, and it had been sent on its way some weeks before. However, due to a typo in the address, it went on a merry-go-round to several other countries before reaching Singapore a day before recording! It was very frightening, really, and we were imagining what state it would be in upon arrival. I was also wondering whose violin to borrow for the recording should it not be playable.

Thankfully, it was carefully checked and prepared for the recording immediately upon arrival and ready to make music. It was larger than my current three-quarter size, so I remember practising on it for hours the night before, trying to get used to the new size, weight, and feel. There was definitely a little anxiety there!

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by THE VIOLINIST (@violinistmovie)

What was it like watching the finished film for the first time and hearing your own playing come from a character on screen? Was there a moment that particularly stayed with you?

It was so surreal. I would never have imagined hearing my own playing in a film, and I felt nervous as the scenes approached, but I think it went well after all.

I particularly enjoyed the duet where Fei and Kai first play together after he has been secretly taking lessons with the teacher, and the comedic comment the teacher had made about her salary.

If you’re comfortable sharing, what does playing the violin for your father at his bedside mean to you, especially now that music has become such a personal form of connection for your family?

My father was the one shuttling me to and fro violin class since I was in preschool. He was always so happy to hear me practise at home, although most classical music made him yawn. Sometimes he’d give me song requests and show me the YouTube clips. Because I play by ear, he was always so thrilled to hear me replay his favourite songs on the spot.

Funny memory: I remember once when I was lazy and refused to practise that day. He made me hold the empty violin case over my head for some time! Don’t worry, it just happened once.

Now that he is in hospital, it’s time for me to do what I can for my father. Mum plays the recording of the Sunset Sonata performance for him to hear, and I play the violin for him at times by the bedside. Even if he cannot express it, I know he can hear it, as there are responsive signs from him each time.

When we are not there, we leave a mobile phone with different genres of music playing for him several hours a day — from classical music to The Beatles to old songs of P. Ramlee.

Finally, after experiencing music through competitions, major stages, arranging, composing, film, and something so personal, has your answer changed when someone asks you: “Why do you play the violin?”

The enduring reason why I play the violin is because I enjoy seeing the looks of delight on people’s faces as they hear me play live and knowing that I have made someone smile that day.

BABYMONSTER have wrapped up two sold-out nights at Kyocera Dome Osaka, welcoming 90,000 fans to the latest stop of their world tour. The K-pop girl group took over the venue on 22 and 23 September, marking their first-ever performances at the dome.

As the lights went down, fans across the venue rose to their feet to welcome BABYMONSTER, whose opening performance of 'WE GO UP' kicked off the night with a full live band and the members performing with handheld microphones.

The group kept the energy going with 'SHEESH' and 'DRIP', both of which have surpassed 100 million cumulative streams in Japan, alongside tracks from their third mini-album, 춤 (CHOOM).

For the special dome shows, BABYMONSTER expanded their setlist with 'Ghost', their first original Japanese song, viral track 'REALLY LIKE YOU', and latest release 'SUGAR HONEY ICE TEA'. Individual solo stages also gave each member a chance to spotlight their vocals, rap, and performance skills.

The scale of the dome was matched by an equally massive production. Cinematic VCRs punctuated the set, while lasers, pyrotechnics, fog, and a sprawling stage transformed the venue throughout the night. Across the stands, fans added to the spectacle with waves of synchronised light sticks.

BABYMONSTER also spent plenty of time connecting directly with their Japanese fans. The members spoke in Japanese throughout the concert without interpreters and even worked Osaka dialect into their interactions with the crowd.

During the encore, the group boarded moving carts to get closer to fans around the dome. The audience's response eventually brought BABYMONSTER back out for a second encore, extending the celebration through one final round of performances.

The concerts capped off the group's Japan tour, which began in Kobe in July and comprised 11 shows across six cities. A total of 200,000 fans attended the run, while the finale at Kyocera Dome Osaka was broadcast live via WOWOW.

The dome debut also marked an emotional milestone for the group. Japanese members ASA and RUKA reflected on seeing the venue filled with fans after finally reaching a stage they had long dreamed of performing on.

"From the very first moment onstage, we felt so overwhelmed that we thought we might cry. Seeing the fans fill every seat made us realise once again just how many people love us," they shared.

"Every one of these moments is possible thanks to all our fans, who have always supported us without wavering. We hope to continue moving forward with you and create even more wonderful memories together."

The milestone follows BABYMONSTER's growing live presence in Japan, from attracting 46,000 attendees to their first fan meeting in 2024 to drawing 250,000 in 2025. With another 200,000 attendees across this year's Japan tour, their cumulative live attendance in the country is now approaching 500,000.

BABYMONSTER launched their second world tour, 2026-27 BABYMONSTER WORLD TOUR [춤 (CHOOM)], in Seoul in June. The group are set to continue the tour across Asia, Oceania, South America, North America, and Europe, with 30 shows across 18 cities planned in total. An additional Hong Kong concert has also been confirmed for 10 January.

Lola Amour and Jan Roberts are looking back at what could have been in their first collaboration, 'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)'.

Released on 25 September, the folk-pop track sees the two Filipino acts reexamine a relationship that has already ended, turning memories into imagined scenarios and unanswered questions about how things might have turned out differently.

Rather than simply yearning for a former love, 'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)' finds its narrator confronting the lingering "what ifs" that follow a breakup — including the possibility of a life where the relationship never ended.

The song was written by Roberts and Lola Amour frontman Pio Dumayas, with the composition credited to Roberts alongside Lola Amour members Jeffrey Abueg, Emilio Dumayas, Pio, Zoe Gonzales, Angelo Mesina, Raffy Perez, and David Yuhico.

Produced by Lola Amour, the track was recorded by Macoy Manuel, mixed by CUURLEY, and mastered by Jett Galindo. It also features Roi Mendones on trumpet.

'Tapos Na Ba (Tayong Dalawa)' arrives as Lola Amour continue to bring their blend of pop, funk, and indie music to audiences beyond the Philippines. The seven-piece are set to return to Singapore for the Singapore Formula 1 Grand Prix, joining a lineup that includes Janet Jackson, Goo Goo Dolls, Zara Larsson, CORTIS, and more.

Roberts, meanwhile, released his debut five-track EP, Pusong Pabrika, in August. The project was preceded by 'Selepono' with jikamarie and 'Kung Masusunod' with Johnoy Danao, the latter of which is nominated for Folk Song of the Year at the 2026 Filipino Music Awards.

Gehlee Dangca is coming home. After three years of living and pursuing her dreams in South Korea, the Filipina singer and former UNIS member will return to the Philippines on 29 September as she begins a new chapter in her career as a solo artist.

Gehlee is set to pursue opportunities both in the Philippines and internationally, while also returning home to finish school. Fans can expect to see more of the young artist across Philippine media and entertainment through upcoming appearances, projects, and activities.

Gehlee first caught international attention through Universe Ticket, the global survival programme that formed K-pop girl group UNIS. Her journey began after SBS approached Universal Records Philippines to scout Filipino talents for the competition.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by gehlee 🌸 (@gehlee_dangca)

After securing a spot on the programme, Gehlee emerged as one of its standout contestants, garnering the highest number of votes and ultimately taking the fourth debut spot among the eight members selected for UNIS.

She officially debuted with the group in March 2024 and spent the next two and a half years based in South Korea, building her experience as a performer and K-pop artist while reaching audiences around the world.

With her return to the Philippines, Gehlee will continue working with Universal Records Philippines as her recording label. GLXY Talent Management, the talent management arm of Universal Records, and Star Horizon TV Production will oversee her management in the Philippines.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by GLXY Talent Management (@glxymanagement)

Both management teams have supported Gehlee's career since before her time in South Korea and will continue working together to develop opportunities for the singer locally.

Gehlee also joins Universal Records and GLXY's growing roster of international talents, which includes Korean stars Kim Myung Soo (L) and Choi Bo Min, as well as Thai internet personality Aon Somrutai.

With international performing experience under her belt, Gehlee's homecoming will give her a chance to reconnect with Filipino fans while continuing to build her career beyond the Philippines. More details on Gehlee's upcoming projects, media appearances, and activities are expected to be announced soon.

items.body: DUKE ELLINGTON & JOHN COLTRANE - s/t (Impulse!, 1963) By Ferruccio Martinotti Sunday morning. We weren't even looking through Trane’s records, we already had a clear plan for the centenary. Then we spotted it. Or rather, it was almost as if IT was looking at us. There it was, humble and elusive amidst some truly gigantic "neighbors": “Duke Ellington & John Coltrane”. When a title says it all. How long had it been since it last took a spin on the turntable? A long, long time. So, we not only dusted it off, rescuing it from obscurity and oblivion but also cast it as the star of our own humble contribution to the Coltrane forum’s tribute. A quick preamble. Our favorite Trane is the one who burned all his bridges behind and embarked on the Path of Spiritual Ascension alongside Alice, Pharoah, Garrison, and Ali: for us, THIS is John’s definitive group. Since we are certain that our colleagues will, as usual, handle albums like ‘Interstellar Space”, “Olatunji”, “Live in Japan” et al, with the utmost mastery, we opted for a record you won’t find on "100 all-time best" playlists or among the essential albums by either Duke or Trane, yet one that is nonetheless deeply compelling. First things first: when and how did this encounter (the only one, if we’re not mistaken) between two of the greatest musicians of all time take place? The date: September 26, 1962. The setting: Rudy Van Gelder’s Studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, a place so legendary that, like Atlantis, one wonders if it ever truly existed. The mastermind: Bob Thiele, a producer at Impulse! The Maestri arrived at the meeting from different trajectories, not just in terms of age, but artistically as well. Duke, at 63, as the old king of the jungle, having already changed the course of music history in the 1920s and 30s, he wanted to show the "young lions" that the time to end up in the zoo hadn't arrived just yet. And judging by the extraordinary “Money Jungle”, recorded right some weeks earlier along with Max Roach and Charles Mingus, he had every right to feel that way. Trane, meanwhile, aged 35, was in a transitional phase. Leading one of jazz’s most sensational lineups ever (Jones, Garrison, Tyner), he had just released his first album for Impulse! in 1962, a record where modal structures were handled sublimely, yet he had not entirely cut ties with a more “mainstream” approach to his music (though, given the musical context, quotation marks are essential here!). It was as if, mid-journey, he had paused to catch his breath and look back one last time, before lighting the fuse and blowing everything wide open. The two arrived at the studio bringing their respective rhythm sections: Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones for Coltrane; Aaron Bell and Sam Woodyard from Ellington’s orchestra. To glimpse a moment of that historic occasion, we can turn to bassist John Lamb, who was present that day: “There was no music on that whole date. Nobody had a chart. We came in and we were standing there, waiting to see what would have happen. Trane would go and sit on the piano bench with Duke. They didn’t talk but Duke would be singing and Trane would go. Then, after they did that for a few minutes, they got up. Trane would go to his microphone, Duke would start playing and the rhythm section, we had to do for ourselves, you know. That’s it. He didn’t even tell you the key. He could communicate without words and Trane could hear it.” The eight-hour session yielded seven tracks: “In a Sentimental Mood”, “Take The Coltrane” and “Stevie” (two sketches composed right there in the studio), “Angelica” and “The Feeling of Jazz” by Ellington; Billy Strayhorn’s “My Little Brown Book”; and Coltrane’s “Big Nick,” a tribute to tenor saxophonist Big Nick Nicholas. At work here are two living legends who set out not to change history, but simply to experience, with mutual respect and admiration, the intimate joy of music. No overbearing displays, no pointless academic showing-off or gratuitous virtuosity. Pure Magic. Even Elvin Jones puts down the sticks of dynamite and picks up the brushes. It is a "Sunday Morning Record", relaxed, atmospheric, and straightforward, reminding us that in our constant search for the ultimate, mind-blowing thrill (which, by definition, is NEVER the last one), we often lose sight of the wonder of simplicity. This is the perfect album to set that right. Let us leave the final word on this experience to Trane: “I was really honored to have the opportunity of working with Duke. It was a wonderful experience. He has set standards I haven’t caught up with yet. I would have liked to have worked over all those numbers again, but I guess the performances wouldn’t have had the same spontaneity. And they mightn’t have been any better.” May the Journey be light for you, dear John. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online.
